Nevada Finalizes Sweeping Overhaul of Its Gaming Technical Standards

Published November 17, 2026 · 3 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

The Nevada Gaming Control Board has finalized extensive revisions to the state's Technical Standards for Gaming Devices and Associated Equipment, the rulebook covering back-end systems used by slot machines, keno, payment processing, sportsbooks, and related equipment across the state's casinos. Board Chair Mike Dreitzer notified licensees that the overhaul was finalized after reviewing public comments and recommendations gathered during the rulemaking process.

What's changing, and when

The revisions consolidate standards that had previously been scattered across multiple separate documents, some of which hadn't been updated in years, into a single, more current set of rules. The board posted drafts of ten standards for public review in September, held a workshop on October 7, and closed the second comment period on November 15 before finalizing the package. The new standards take effect December 13, 2026, but licensees have until October 1, 2027, to come into full compliance — a roughly ten-month runway intended to give operators and equipment manufacturers time to adjust systems and documentation.

Why the board made the change

According to the board, the project had been in development for years, driven by industry complaints that the existing standards were fragmented and difficult to interpret correctly. Jeremy Eberwein, the board's chief of technology, said the goal was to give licensees and manufacturers a single resource they can reference directly rather than having to interpret how older rules apply to current technology — addressing, in his words, questions the board had fielded repeatedly over the past decade.

Why it matters to the industry

Technical standards like these govern how equipment manufacturers get new slot machines, payment systems, and related gaming technology certified for use in Nevada, one of the most closely watched gaming jurisdictions in the country given how often other states model their own rules on Nevada's framework. A consolidated, modernized standard can streamline approval timelines for new equipment, though the lengthy compliance runway means casino visitors and players aren't likely to notice any immediate change on the floor. The update also arrives during a period of transition for the board itself: Chair Dreitzer's term expires in late January 2027, around the same time Nevada's incoming attorney general takes office, leaving open whether current board members are reappointed.
